name: GABON

flag.title: Flag of Gabon
flag.note: Green, yellow & blue — forest, sun, ocean

lead: Gabon sits on Africa's Atlantic coast, where the Equator crosses ancient rainforest. Over 80% of the land is jungle. Forest elephants, silverback gorillas and mandrills live there.

facts.label: Land area
facts.sub: about the size of New Zealand

sections.geography: A forest on the ocean's edge
sections.wows: 7 things to make you go wow

geo: Rainforest covers over 80% of Gabon. The Ogooué River winds 1,200 km to the sea.
The coast has white-sand beaches, mangrove swamps and rocky coves. Inland, the hills of the Chaillu Massif hold Lopé National Park, a World Heritage Site.
animals: Gabon shelters nearly 85,000 forest elephants, more than any other country. In Loango National Park, they stroll along the beach.
The mandrill is the world's largest monkey, with a vivid red-and-blue face. It is Gabon's national animal. Around 35,000 western lowland gorillas live in the forests.
culture: Gabon has more than 40 ethnic groups. The largest is the Fang. The Bwiti spiritual tradition mixes ancestor worship, drumming and the sacred iboga plant, a forest shrub.
Music fills village life. The mvet harp-lute and the wooden obala xylophone set the beat at festivals.
history: Portuguese sailors arrived in 1472. They named the river mouth 'Gabão' for its cloak-like shape. France took control of Gabon in the 1800s. Freed enslaved people founded Libreville, which means 'free town'.
Gabon won independence on 17 August 1960. Oil money in the 1970s made it one of Africa's richer nations. In 2021 it became the first African country paid cash to protect its forests.
wows: Gabon soaks up more CO₂ (a heat-trapping gas) than it makes, as few countries on Earth do.
In Loango National Park you can see beach elephants, surfing hippos and whales on the same day.
Gabon made the iboga plant a national treasure in 2000, now studied as a possible addiction treatment.
In 2002 Gabon created 13 national parks at once, protecting 11% of its land.
Forest elephants are 'mega-gardeners' that spread seeds far and wide in their dung.
Lopé has 1,800 ancient rock carvings alongside gorillas, a rare natural and cultural UNESCO site.
Gabon's flag has a rare 3:4 shape, shared by only DR Congo, Papua New Guinea and San Marino.

myths.fact: Gorillas are shy plant-eaters. Chest-beating is a show to warn rivals, and real fights are rare.

myths.myth: All African elephants are the same
myths.fact: Forest elephants are a separate species. They are smaller than savanna elephants and have straighter tusks.
